abstract: 5-Azacytidine (5-AzaC) is a cytidine analog chemotherapeutic widely used to treat myeloid malignancies. Although its activity is primarily attributed to DNA hypomethylation, the majority of 5-AzaC is incorporated into RNA, where its functional consequences are less understood. Here, we show that 5-AzaC treatment of cells leads to inhibition of protein synthesis. Ribo-seq, Disome-seq, and RNA-seq in treated cells exhibit a time-dependent C-to-G conversion in mRNAs. These conversion events are enriched within footprint positions corresponding to the A-site of monosomes or stalled leading ribosomes in a disome complex. Footprints are accumulated at sites with C-rich codons in the A-site, with particular emphasis on the second codon position. Consistent with disome-mediated signaling, 5-AzaC activates ZAK- and GCN2-dependent stress responses. Furthermore, loss of the ribosome-associated quality control factor, ZNF598, sensitizes cells to 5-AzaC. These findings suggest that translation disruption represents an additional layer of 5-AzaC's mechanism of action, alongside its known DNA-mediated effects.
